To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
access to trans-specific healthcare in the Swedish context is stratified based on the ability to adopt a charge taking role and on economic resources.

access to gender-confirmering medical procedures is stratificated based on the ability to adopt a charge taking role, economic and geographic conditions, and a lack of support from the healthcare system.
trans-specific healthcare is difficult to navigate and negotiate, and that this is connected to a shift in responsibility from care-providing institutions to care-users.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which trans-specific care-users' experiences are shaped by neoliberal and technoscientific developments.
the need for a critical analysis of the relationship between neoliberal and biomedical developments within trans-specific care.
the experiences of care-users and how they navigate the biomedical gaze.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the participants' experiences of trans-specific care were characterised by a lack of support and a shift of responsibilities from the healthcare system to the users.

the current trans-specific healthcare in the western world is not only biomedicalised, but that it is neoliberalised and stratified as well, and that this has to be taken into consideration when discussing access to care.
the experiences of the participants are a result of the interplay between neoliberal and technoscientific developments and the lack of resources within Swedish trans-specific care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
trans-specific care is not only a biomedical issue but also a political and social matter.
the current system is not working, and that it needs to be changed.
the participants' experiences of trans-specific healthcare can be seen as an example of how neoliberal developments in healthcare are intertwined with biomedicalisation and stratify access to care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biomedical gaze is not only a matter of surveillance, but also a matter of responsibility.
the current system is not only difficult to navigate, but also that it is not designed to be navigated.
care-seekers are not only affected by the biomedicalisation of trans-specific care but also by neoliberal developments within healthcare.
